desc:
A dictionary stores the keys 1, 2, ..., n in a binary search tree. Key i + 1 will be looked up freq[i] times. Looking up a key costs its depth in the tree, where the root has depth 1, its children depth 2, and so on.

Among all binary search trees that store these n keys, find the smallest possible total cost, that is the minimum of the sum of freq[i] × depth(key i + 1) over all keys.

Example 1

freq = [34,8,50]
Output: 142
Key 3 as root (cost 50), key 1 as its left child (cost 34 × 2) and key 2 below it as the right child (8 × 3): 50 + 68 + 24 = 142.

Example 2

freq = [3,3,3]
Output: 15
The middle key as root: 3 + 6 + 6.
hints: Choosing the root splits the keys into a left part and a right part, each of which becomes a subtree. What happens to the depth of every key in those parts?

Every key in a subtree is one level deeper than it would be as the root of that subtree, which adds exactly the total frequency of the subtree to its cost. Define the cost of a key interval [i, j) and try all roots r in it.

cost[i][j] = min over r of (cost[i][r] + cost[r+1][j]) + sum(freq[i..j-1]). Prefix sums give interval sums in O(1). Trying all roots is O(n³); to get O(n²) note that the best root of [i, j) lies between the best root of [i, j-1) and the best root of [i+1, j) (Knuth's optimization).
editorial: For the key interval [i, j) let cost[i][j] be the minimum total cost of a BST on exactly these keys. If key r is the root, the cost is its own frequency plus the cost of both subtrees, and every key of both subtrees moves one level deeper, which adds their frequencies once more. In total cost[i][j] = minr(cost[i][r] + cost[r+1][j]) + W(i, j) where W is the sum of frequencies in the interval (a prefix-sum difference). The empty interval costs 0.

Filling the table by increasing interval length gives O(n³), fine up to a few hundred keys in a compiled language. The cost function satisfies the quadrangle inequality, so the optimal root is monotone: opt[i][j-1] ≤ opt[i][j] ≤ opt[i+1][j]. Restricting the search for r to that window makes the work along each diagonal telescope, giving O(n²) time overall with O(n²) memory.
